sim.title: What a camera sees of the horizon, in true projection
sim.mini: The sea seen by a camera at the height and lens printed in the image. Green: the globe's horizon, a ring at the dip δ ≈ √(2h/R) below eye level. Orange dashes: eye level, where a plane's horizon would lie. From 35,000 ft over 62.7°: {{lynchRef}} of bend; measured {{lynchMeas}}.
sim.text: Every pixel is coloured by the direction it looks in: sea below the horizon, sky above, for the height, field of view and lens printed in the top-left corner. The solid green line is the globe's horizon with standard refraction, the Earth's radius R replaced by R/(1 − k) with k = 0.13 [3][4]; the thin white dashes are the same horizon without refraction. That horizon is a ring at the dip δ ≈ √(2h/R) below eye level [2][3], so across a field 2a wide it bends by only about δ·a²/2; the dotted chord and the short vertical stroke mark that sagitta. The orange dashes are eye level, where the horizon of an infinite plane would lie. An ordinary lens, r = f·tan θ, keeps that line straight anywhere in the frame; a fish-eye or a strong wide-angle bends it as soon as it is off the centre, and that bend is the lens, not the Earth [5]. True projection, no exaggeration; the line under the image gives the dip, the radius of the ring along the ground and the sagitta on a photograph 4,000 pixels wide with the same field. From 35,000 ft, horizon centred, over 62.7°, Lynch measured {{lynchMeas}} on a photograph [1]; the globe gives {{lynchRef}} with refraction, {{lynchGeo}} without.
sim.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a sea horizon that stays at eye level as the camera climbs, or a centred photo from high altitude with an ordinary lens and no sagitta at all.
depth.title: Why the curve shows in depth, not left to right
depth.mini: The Turning Torso, 190 m, filmed across the sea from 2 m: at 47.9 km, {{tHidF}} of it is hidden behind the water; climbing to 17.6 m brings {{tBackF2}} back. From the same spot, the horizon across a 90° lens bends by {{s90eye}} on a 4,000-pixel photo.
depth.text: On 26 February 2016 the Turning Torso in Malmö, 190 m tall, was filmed across the Øresund from 25 to 47.9 km, eye 2 to 4 m above the water, then from 17.6 m [1]. Left, the camera's view in true perspective; right, the same instant in profile; the red line is the hidden height the author measured on each shot [2]. The hidden part grows with the square of the distance, H = (d − √(2Rh))²/2R: at 47.9 km {{tHidF}} is gone, against {{tGeoF}} for a globe without refraction; the refraction that fits each shot runs from {{kMin}} to {{kMax}}. A plane hides nothing. The horizon is a ring at the dip δ ≈ √(2h/R) below eye level and bends only by about δ·a²/2 across a field 2a wide: {{s90eye}} on a 4,000-pixel photo through a 90° lens at 2.1 m, {{s90back}} from {{dpBack}}, {{s90jet}} from an airliner, {{s90iss}} from 400 km. In the profile the Earth is drawn up to 2,000 times smaller and ground distances about 45 times shorter, at uniform scale, so every height is the real one; the factors are printed.
depth.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a distant building whose base stays in view as the camera moves away at constant height, over calm water.
simset.title: The horizon from any height: the camera, the profile, the two formulas
simset.labels: What the camera records|The same height, in profile|The sagitta s = f·tan δ·(sec a − 1)|Hidden height H and the dip δ
simset.mini: Top: a camera's view of the sea at the height printed, and the same height in profile. Bottom: the two formulas. The horizon is a ring δ ≈ √(2h/R) below eye level and bends only by δ·a²/2 across a field 2a wide; on a plane it stays at eye level.
simset.text: Top left, what a camera records at the height, field of view and lens printed in its corner, in true projection: sea below the horizon, sky above; solid green, the globe's horizon with standard refraction (R replaced by R/(1 − k), k = 0.13) [3][4]; white dashes, without refraction; orange dashes, eye level, where the horizon of an infinite plane would lie. Top right, the same height in profile: the ground falls below the level line by d²/2R, and the sightlines that graze it touch the sea on a ring, all at the dip δ below eye level; the Earth is drawn smaller at uniform scale when needed, the factor is printed and the angles are the real ones. Bottom left: a ray at angle a from the axis meets the sensor at f·sec a, so the horizon at the edges of the frame lies f·tan δ·sec a below eye level against f·tan δ at the centre; it bows by s = f·tan δ·(sec a − 1) ≈ δ·a²/2. Bottom right: the dip δ ≈ √(2h/R) [2][3], the horizon distance d₀ = √(2Rh) and the hidden height H = (d − d₀)²/2R of a target at distance d. An ordinary lens keeps the plane's line straight anywhere; a fish-eye bends it off the centre, and that bend is the lens [5]. From 35,000 ft, horizon centred, over 62.7°, Lynch measured {{lynchMeas}} [1]; the globe gives {{lynchRef}} with refraction, {{lynchGeo}} without. The two schematics are not to scale.
simset.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a sea horizon that stays at eye level as the camera climbs, a distant base that stays in view at constant height, or a centred photo from high altitude with an ordinary lens and no sagitta at all.
fx-sag.title: Why the horizon bends so little: s = f·tan δ·(sec a − 1)
fx-sag.mini: The horizon lies δ below eye level, δ ≈ √(2h/R). A ray at angle a from the axis meets the sensor at f·sec a, so the edges sit lower: s = f·tan δ·(sec a − 1) ≈ δ·a²/2. Two small factors multiply.
fx-sag.text: Seen from a height h, the sea horizon lies at the dip δ below eye level: cos δ = R/(R + h), about √(2h/R) [2][3], {{dipBeach}} at 2 m, {{dipJet}} at 35,000 ft. In a level camera of focal length f (in pixels), the centre of the horizon falls f·tan δ below eye level. A ray at angle a from the optical axis travels f·sec a to the sensor plane, so at the edge of the frame the same horizon lies f·tan δ·sec a below eye level. The difference is the sagitta, s = f·tan δ·(sec a − 1) ≈ δ·a²/2 as an angle: two small factors multiplied, the dip growing only as the square root of the height, and a²/2 only 0.14 for a 60° field, 0.31 for 90°. From 35,000 ft, horizon centred, over 62.7°, Lynch measured {{lynchMeas}} [1]; the globe gives {{lynchRef}} with refraction, {{lynchGeo}} without. The drawing is not to scale: its angles are enlarged.
fx-sag.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a sea horizon that stays at eye level as the observer climbs, with a dip of zero at every height.
fx-hid.title: Hidden height and dip: H = (d − d₀)²/2R
fx-hid.mini: From an eye at height h the sea horizon lies d₀ = √(2Rh) away, δ ≈ √(2h/R) below eye level. A target at distance d loses its lower H = (d − d₀)²/2R behind the water. On a plane, H = 0 at any distance.
fx-hid.text: Left, in profile: from an eye at height h, the line of sight that grazes the sea touches it at the horizon, d₀ = √(2Rh) away. Beyond it the surface keeps falling, and a target at distance d has its lower part H = (d − d₀)²/2R below that line, hidden by the water. The same tangent sets the dip, δ ≈ √(2h/R) below eye level [3]. Right, in the photograph: the horizon lies δ below the dashed eye level and arches up by the sagitta s ≈ δ·a²/2 across half the field a. The first grows with the square of the distance, the second with the square root of the height: depth shows the curvature, left to right hardly does. On 26 February 2016 the Turning Torso in Malmö, 190 m tall, filmed across the Øresund from 2 to 4 m, had {{tHidF}} hidden at 47.9 km [1][2], against {{tGeoF}} for a globe without refraction; the refraction that fits each shot runs from {{kMin}} to {{kMax}}. The drawing is not to scale: its curvature is enlarged.
fx-hid.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a distant building whose base stays in view as the camera moves away at constant height, over calm water.
